Name: -1_forecast_2025_2026_trend
Representative_Docs: ["on inflation, the outlook is a well-below-consensus disinflation call. core pce stalled at 2.8% year-over-year in 2025, but the note attributes the residual overshoot to one-time tariffs and mostly complete catch-up inflation. ** sees core pce falling to 2.1% by end-2026 — 30bp under both consensus and the fomc — driven by a fading tariff boost (0.5pp now to 0.2pp by december), shelter slowing from 3.7% to 2.3% (below its pre-pandemic pace), and wage growth already at target-consistent levels.** cpi should slightly undershoot pce given shelter's larger cpi weight and cpi-specific insurance declines, putting the headline cpi call at 2.1% q4/q4 — 30bp below market pricing and 60bp below consensus.", 'the bottom line is that method changes the level but not the conclusion. **across essentially all g10 curves both models show term premium elevated and near local highs, implying only modest increases in rate expectations outside australia, the uk and japan.** the persistence of high premium alongside falling implied volatility — usually a combination that would compress premium — points to a structural rise in duration risk premium tied to fiscal, growth and inflation risks and shrinking central bank balance sheets, rather than to cyclical swings or bond-supply weakness alone. the note flags deeper work on drivers and valuation to come, and offers no explicit trade idea.', 'on positioning, a return to fed easing is expected to lower treasury yields and the dollar while lifting global equities and gold. **the stated preference is short dollar and long gold, since both also hedge fed-independence and renewed-tariff risks.** rate views across the euro area, uk, canada and australia sit mostly on the dovish side of market pricing; the commodity team raised its near-term oil forecast on low oecd inventories but still sees lower prices medium-term as spare capacity stays high and opec cuts unwind.']

Name: 0_inflation_economy_2026_2025
Representative_Docs: ['since the july meeting, **the fomc\'s center of gravity has clearly shifted toward a september cut**, anchored in powell\'s jackson hole remarks that policy in restrictive territory, combined with the shift in the balance of risks, may justify adjusting the stance. waller is the most explicit: he wants to "get ahead" of the labor market and would support 25bp in september, signaling 100-150bp of cuts over the next 3-6 months, with the pace — every meeting or every other meeting — data-dependent. bostic converges on "around 25bp" for the rest of the year, and williams acknowledges it will become appropriate to move the rate toward neutral.', '**a 25bp cut at the september fomc is expected to be the first of three this year, with further 25bp moves in october and december and two more in 2026, taking the funds rate to 3–3.25%.** the fomc statement is not expected to nod toward an october cut, though powell may hint softly at consecutive cuts in the press conference. the dot plot is projected to show two cuts in 2025 to 3.875% (by a narrow 10-9 majority), two more in 2026 to 3.375%, one in 2027 to 3.125%, no change in 2028, and an unchanged 3% neutral rate.', "the calendar's anchor is the **january fomc minutes on wednesday, which will read for detail on participants' views of the appropriate policy stance and the path ahead.** powell's press conference already set the frame: policy is still restrictive, the committee is in no rush, and once the policy backdrop from the new administration is clearer, the bar for another cut is not high on further inflation progress. reads this as ruling out march and keeps its base case of cuts in june and december, then one more in 2026."]

the 10y bund forecast stays at 3.0% for end-2025, with rising net supply and ecb qt slowing the pace of spread tightening. **oat spreads are expected to hold their range — 70bp at year-end — because the hurdle for deficit or growth expectations to deteriorate against already-low market pricing is high.** eur vol is judged to have fallen about as far as fundamentals justify at the front, while long-end vol stays elevated on global long-end uncertainty and dutch pension reform, and should keep trading directionally with the curve.', 'in europe, the improvement is modest but the front-end risk balance has shifted. two more ecb cuts are expected, but with a higher terminal rate the case for longs has weakened. **the german curve now carries a clear signature: the level moves with risk sentiment and near-term growth, but the trend reflects fiscal expectations — justifying a steep eur front-end.** within egbs, sovereign credit longs are preferred to core rates, and southern europe should keep outperforming, supported by ecb policy space and german willingness to spend. deeper btp/bonos tightening, though, would require durable foreign inflows to offset ecb qt, and that likely needs lower french political risk.']

Name: 7_inflation_recession_outperformance_fiscal
Representative_Docs: ['**the durability of long-end forward-curve steepness rests on a dampened convexity benefit and higher yields abroad, not just a steeper curve further in.** the 5y5y/10y20y slope can be explained by the inner forward slope, implied vol, and the relative level of 5y5y yields abroad versus the us. lower vol has cut the convexity benefit to longer yields; relatively higher foreign yields did the rest. if the fed shift brings a steeper curve plus higher long-end vol, the back-end effects roughly offset; persistently higher term premium without more rate vol would push long-end yields higher still.', "on the us curve, the preferred expression is anchoring longs in the 5y. **the 5y sits at the intersection of two forces — greater scope for 2s5s flattening if inflation surprises up, and stickier long-end forwards that lag in rallies — even after pockets of belly underperformance in the oil-driven move higher in yields.** traded inflation is caught between rising oil and hawkish fedspeak plus benign june cpi; longer-term forwards screen modestly cheap while 1y1y and 2y2y trade rich on oil sensitivity, but with the economists' baseline for softer-than-priced 12-to-18-month inflation, traded inflation is not seen as a compelling outright long.", '**belly breakevens are singled out as the more reliable hedge for fed uncertainty than nominal rates.** the response of front-end and belly nominals to fed headlines has been mixed, but 5y inflation swaps have repriced consistently higher, with belly forwards such as 2y1y participating. the ~15bp richness to fair value is described as historically unremarkable. the key asymmetry is that the long-end has not followed: 5y5y inflation stays soft, so the market is pricing near-term inflation risk without lifting the long-term premium.']

Name: 10_outperformance_spillovers_market_inflation
Representative_Docs: ['the uk story is the mirror image of the us. **the "rising yields, falling currency" pattern that raised gilt risk premium in recent years is no longer clearly a uk feature, with the baton passed to treasuries.** an improving inflation outlook relaxes the constraint on both monetary and fiscal policy, easing the path to boe cuts and compressing gilt curve risk premium — hence the call for long-end gilts to outperform usts.', 'gilts are the clearest event trade. weak services inflation, retail sales and pmis barely moved yields beyond cementing a december boe cut, leaving the market frozen ahead of the budget. **the base case is that gilts have priced enough event risk premium, and a contractionary, non-inflationary budget clears the way for lower yields as boe easing expectations build.** the focus is threefold: borrowing roughly £8bn above the spring figure with matching gilt sales, the credibility and front-loading of revenue measures, and the macro/boe implications. the book favours long gilts (e.g. versus bunds) and adds long 10y gilt on asw (entry −52bp, target −44bp, stop −57bp); the 2s5s gilt steepener is closed for a 10bp gain.', "- **gilts should continue to see risk premium compression, supporting the long 10-year position.** the initial reaction was ambiguous — tension between larger headroom and delayed tightening — but relief prevailed, reinforced by the dmo's decision to shift issuance away from 30-year gilts more than expected. the 30-year-led bull-flattening and the positive correlation between gilts and sterling indicate that risk-premium compression is the dominant driver, not a change in the expected boe path. the read is that the market had been pricing excessive risk premium relative to the macro backdrop; with the event past, focus should shift to weak activity and inflation data and to boe decisions, with disinflation pulling front-end rates lower. long positions in 10-year gilts versus bunds and ois are maintained, along with year-end forecasts of 4.25% for end-2025 and 4.0% for end-2026."]

Name: 75_finance_spillovers_leverage_investors
Representative_Docs: ['**for the reader, the takeaway is that private credit is a contained risk to watch, not a systemic trigger — and the real tail sits in the wider price of credit.** bank lending to business is accelerating, corporate balance sheets are healthy, and ai investment demand supports credit growth, all of which cushion a private-credit retreat. the scenario that would matter more is a broad widening of credit spreads, whether from ai-related uncertainty or a general tightening in financial conditions.', '- a private-credit distress scenario with loan losses rising to 5% (vs. a ~2% historical average) reduces growth by ~0.2pp, a contained hit given private credit is only ~5% of nonfinancial private-sector credit.', 'the stress test then asks what happens if private credit loan losses climb to between 3.5% (the covid-era rate) and 7.5% (the 2008 peak for private-equity-sponsored loans). key assumptions: banks rebuild to their original capital ratio with half the adjustment coming through reduced lending, nbfis pull back in line with historical behavior — banks cut lending more than nbfis on average, though insurers and pension funds react less and mutual funds and finance companies more — a 33% recovery rate, and a 0.4 elasticity of borrower spending to lending. **the outcome is modest: a 0.3–1.2% hit to economywide lending and 0.1–0.5% to gdp, implying private credit is not a meaningful macro risk even accounting for interconnections.** the result hinges on how concentrated the shock is — losses spread evenly across funds hit only equity investors, since sector capital exceeds even the 7.5% scenario, while losses concentrated in a few undercapitalized funds reach their lenders and bite harder.']

Representative_Docs: ['at issue. this daily answers three recurring investor questions following \'s earlier work on payment-stablecoin adoption and its implications for the us financial system, safe-asset demand, and treasury issuance. the questions: (1) how stablecoins actually displace deposits when issuer asset purchases seem to recycle funds back into the system; (2) how bank heterogeneity changes those dynamics; and (3) whether foreign "dollarization" via stablecoins is a genuine tailwind for treasuries. no new event or data release — this is a clarification of an existing thesis.', 'payments involve two distinct tools: the asset used (cash, bank deposits, stablecoins, cbdcs) and the payment rail that moves it. a new rail can be built without a new asset — the public fast payment systems do exactly that, running existing deposits or cash over new infrastructure. **the note treats stablecoins and cbdcs as new digital assets and public fast payment systems as new rails, and judges each by how well it overcomes the same network-effect barrier.**', 'backdrop. usd safe assets (short-term treasuries, repos, government mmfs, deposits, central bank reserves) form the collateral base of the financial system, each with a distinct profile of yield, guarantee, and backing. bank deposits pay interest, are insured (up to $250k per account), and are only partially backed by safe assets. government mmfs sit outside the banking system, carry no deposit insurance, and are fully backed by short-maturity safe assets — functioning as an interest-paying "narrow bank." seigniorage — the revenue the central bank earns by issuing non-interest-bearing currency — has historically belonged to the public sector.']

Name: 92_finance_earnings_trend_forecast
Representative_Docs: ["**job growth has slowed to near zero once revisions are included.** nonfarm payrolls fell 23k in july against expectations near +80k, and june and may were revised down by 37k and 66k respectively. this cuts the three-month average to 20k (from 111k) and 's preferred underlying pace — blending payroll and household surveys — to just 5k (from 74k). the weakness is broad but partly seasonal: leisure and hospitality fell 40k and government fell 53k, the latter driven by a 50k drop in local government education that likely reflects school-summer-break patterns not fully captured by seasonal adjustment. healthcare (+23k) and construction (+22k) were the only notable gains, while the diffusion index fell to roughly 51-52. the report fits a recurring pattern of weak july prints and negative revisions seen in each of the last three years.", '**job growth is weak and getting weaker after revisions.** payrolls rose just 50k in december, below the 70k expected, and prior months were revised down sharply — november by 8k and october by 68k, the latter now showing an outright decline of 173k driven by cuts to both federal (-179k) and private-sector figures. private payrolls added only 37k, with a three-month average of 29k. gains concentrated in leisure/hospitality, healthcare, and local government, while retail, construction, and professional services shed jobs; the one-month diffusion index fell to 50.8. adjusting for likely revisions, the shutdown-driven federal drop, and an overstated household-survey population, the estimated underlying pace of hiring is just 11k — below the breakeven rate that holds unemployment steady.', "**payrolls beat, but the strength is concentrated and possibly overstated.** nonfarm payrolls rose 147k (vs. 106k median), with april and may revised up 16k combined, lifting the three-month average to 150k. the gains were narrow — government (+73k), healthcare (+59k), and leisure and hospitality (+20k). an 80k jump in state and local employment, led by 64k in education, is flagged as possibly a seasonal-adjustment artifact: education payrolls normally fall sharply in june with the school year's end, so the seasonally adjusted spike may not reflect real hiring. private payrolls rose just 74k, below expectations, and the diffusion index slipped to 49.6, below its 2019q4 average — signs the breadth of hiring is weak."]
